title: Wedding Money and Home Visits: Tiyatien Health's First Year in Zwedru
dek: In 2007 Raj Panjabi, his wife and Liberian civil war survivors used $6,000 of wedding money to start rural HIV care carried to patients' homes by neighbours.

story.founder: Raj Panjabi, with Amisha Raja, Marcus Kudee, Peter Luckow, Alphonso Mouwon and Weafas Quitoe
story.event: Starting a community-based HIV programme in Zwedru with wedding money and lay accompaniers
story.summary: In 2007 Raj Panjabi and Amisha Raja asked wedding guests for money instead of gifts and, with Liberian civil war survivors and American health workers, used the $6,000 raised to found Tiyatien Health. Its first project, run with Liberia's Ministry of Health at the hospital in Zwedru, Grand Gedeh County, relied on lay accompaniers who carried HIV medicines to patients' homes; by November 2007 it had enrolled more than 70 patients. The organisation, later Last Mile Health, went on to train community health workers in remote districts.
paragraphs: On 2 November 2007, Raj Panjabi posted a short update from Zwedru, a town in Grand Gedeh County in south-eastern Liberia. In its first six months, the HIV Equity Initiative, run by a new group called Tiyatien Health with Liberia's Ministry of Health, had enrolled more than 70 people with HIV; nearly 35 were on antiretroviral drugs. Some patients had gained over 20 kilograms and gone back to work. It was, he wrote, "such a joy to see the reclaiming of lives".

Panjabi had left Liberia at nine, evacuated on a cargo plane as civil war reached Monrovia in 1990, and grew up in North Carolina. Fifteen years later, as a medical student in his mid-20s, he went back. He has said the war left 51 doctors for four million people, and that he saw patients die of treatable illness because they reached him too late. In 2007, the year he married Amisha Raja, the couple asked relatives for money instead of wedding presents. It came to $6,000. With Liberian civil war survivors and American health workers, they founded Tiyatien Health, a name meaning justice in health.

The model rested on neighbours. Accompaniers, chosen by people with HIV or their families and trained by Tiyatien and ministry staff, walked to patients' homes each day with medicines, food and support. Each was also asked to look out for anyone sick nearby; on one round of visits, 17 accompaniers found nearly 150 sick people and sent them to the clinic. Panjabi noted that the town's Tubman Hospital had two government doctors and the rest of the county none. Trained, supervised and paid community health workers could fill part of the gap, he wrote, but doctors were badly needed too.

The approach spread. In 2010, with the government and the Global Fund, the HIV model was copied in 19 public clinics. In 2012 the organisation, later renamed Last Mile Health, began training community health workers in Konobo, a remote district Panjabi had first mentioned in 2007, when a young man from one of its villages was seeking help for a clinic rebuilt from makeshift materials. During the Ebola epidemic of 2014 and 2015 it helped train more than 1,300 health workers.

quote.text: or I do it as well as I can, taking to help me the man who with the aid of my ruling principle can do what is now fit and useful for the general good.
quote.source_title: Thoughts of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, tr. George Long, Project Gutenberg eBook #15877
quote.connection: Marcus, unsure his own powers are enough, resolves to do the work with a helper who can do what is needed. Panjabi did just that with accompaniers, yet his own 2007 note refused the comfort of it: helpers could fill part of the gap, but Liberia still needed doctors.

reflection: What stands out in Panjabi's 2007 notes is how plainly he counted: 70 patients, 35 on treatment, two doctors for a county. He did not pretend that a neighbour with a bag of medicines was the same as a physician. He also did not wait for the physicians to arrive before starting.

You may often be the one with the most training in the room, and the temptation is to carry everything yourself. Sharing a task well means teaching it, supervising it and paying for it fairly, while staying honest about what still needs someone with your skills.
invitation: Choose one routine task you do that someone else could learn. Today, write the three steps you would show them, and note the one point where they would still need to call you.

cross_checks.claim: Panjabi and Amisha Raja raised about $6,000 instead of wedding gifts in 2007 to start the organisation
Its first programme was rural HIV care in Zwedru, run with the Ministry of Health
Panjabi fled Liberia aged nine in 1990 and returned as a medical student
The war had left Liberia with 51 doctors for about four million people
During the Ebola epidemic the organisation helped train more than 1,300 health workers

research_notes: The slate described the 2007 episode as training community health workers in remote Liberia. Contemporary sources show the first project was the HIV Equity Initiative in Zwedru, using lay 'accompaniers'; Last Mile Health's own timeline dates its community health worker pilot in Konobo District to 2012. The story tells the 2007 HIV founding and gives the 2012 community health worker programme as what followed. The TED Blog's line that Last Mile Health has trained community health workers 'since 2007' was not used. Return to Liberia: Panjabi says 15 years after 1990, as a medical student in his mid-20s (TED/NPR), and 'a 24-year-old medical student' with his wife (HMS), which points to about 2005; TIME (2017) says he returned in 2005 'as a doctor', and HMS also says he 'returned in 2007 to found' the organisation. The story says fifteen years later, as a medical student, and dates the founding to 2007. The two 2007 blog posts quoted are signed by Raj; the accompanier posts of 18 and 19 November 2007 are unsigned and are cited only for facts about the programme, not attributed to him. The 'over 70' and 'nearly 35' figures are the blog's own, from October 2007. Size of Liberia's later national programme differs (TIME 2017: more than 4,000 workers planned; Panjabi on NPR 2019: about 3,500 workers and nurses), so no figure is given. The Global Fund replication (19 clinics, 2010) rests on Last Mile Health's timeline. 'Justice in health' is Last Mile Health's and Weill Cornell's translation (Weill Cornell says Krahn). Marcus Aurelius's passage concerns his own fitness for a task; it is applied by analogy. The company field is shortened to 'Tiyatien (later Last Mile)' because the repeat screen treats the shared word Health as the same company and flagged an unrelated 2007 edition (Indus Hospital & Health Network); the prose uses the full names Tiyatien Health and Last Mile Health.
